head.ce:title: Growth of Pseudomonas fluorescens on a polyester–polyurethane and the purification and characterization of a polyurethanase–protease enzyme

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: A Pseudomonas fluorescens was found to degrade and utilize a polyester polyurethane as a sole carbon and energy source. Polyurethane utilization by P. fluorescens. followed simple Michaelis–Menten kinetics. The Ks and μ max values were 0.9 mg ml−1 and 1.61 doublings · h−1, respectively. The enzymes from P. fluorescens responsible for polyurethane degradation were found to be extracellular. Analysis of the polyurethane degrading proteins using non-denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis revealed one active protein band with an Rf value of 0.083. A polyurethane degrading enzyme was purified and displayed protease activity. This enzyme was inhibited by phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride and had a molecular weight of 29,000 daltons.

ce:section.ce:para:
Polyurethanes are an important and versatile class of man-made polymers used in a wide variety of products including paints and coatings, padding and thermal insulating materials. Urethanes are esters of carbonic acid or amide esters of carbonic acid. The urethane linkage results most readily through the reaction of the isocyanate moeity with an alcohol group. The simplest

form is represented by the general formula: (-R-O-C-NH-R′-NH-C-O-)n. The general formula indicates that the hydroxyl-containing component as well as the isocyanate can be changed in a variety of ways to bring about polymers of different characteristics. Microbial degradation of polyurethanes is dependent on the many properties of the polymer such as molecular orientation, crystallinity, cross-linking, and chemical groups present in the molecular chains which determine the accessibility to degrading-enzyme systems. Despite its xenobiotic origins, polyurethane has been found to be susceptible to biodegradation by naturally occurring microorganisms.

It has been suggested by Evans and Levisohn (1968), Hole (1972), Flip (1978), and Griffin (1980)that enzymatic attack on polyurethanes could be contributed by hydrolases such as ureases, proteases, and esterases. Indeed, proteolytic enzymes (papain and urease) and cholesterol esterase have been shown to degrade polyurethanes in vitro (Phua et al., 1987; Santerre et al., 1994).

Many reports have appeared in the literature on the susceptibility of polyurethanes to fungal attack. Mechanisms for this susceptibility have been suggested by Darby and Kaplan (1968)and Kaplan et al. (1968)who have shown that polyester-type polyurethanes are more susceptible to fungal attack than other types of polyurethanes. Four species of fungi, Curvularia sengalensis, Fusarium solani, Aureobasidium pullulans, and Cladosporium sp, were isolated by Crabbe et al. (1994)with the capability of degrading an ester-based polyurethane. C. sengalensis was found to secrete an extracellular enzyme with esterase properties. This enzyme had a molecular weight of 28 kDa and was inhibited by phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride.

In addition to fungal attack, bacteria also contributes to biological degradation of polyurethanes. Blake et al. (manuscript in press) reported bacterial degradation of a polyesterurethane (Impranil DLN) by a Gram positive, Bacillus sp. The pattern of degradation involved the binding of cells to the polymer, the formation of a flocculate, and the degradation of the substrate. This paper reports on the degradation of a polyester-polyurethane by Pseudomonas fluorescens.
P. fluorescens was isolated, identified, and obtained from the Naval Research Laboratory, Washington D.C., by its ability to degrade a water dispersible polyurethane.
P. fluorescens was grown at 30°C in YES medium containing Impranil DLN as previously described (Howard et al., in press)

ce:section.ce:section-title: Determination of number and size of bacterial cells
ce:section.ce:para: P. fluorescens cell number was determined in a Multisizer II instrument (Coulter Scientific Instruments, Inc., Hialeah, FL) fitted with a 30 μm aperture as previously described (Howard et al., in press).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Determination of size distributions of colloidal particles
ce:section.ce:para: Size distribution of Impranil was determined by a LS130 instrument (Coulter Scientific Instruments, Inc., Hialeah, FL). The suspension fluid used was defined YES medium. All experiments were performed at a pump speed of 50%, a PIDS (Polarization Intensity Differential Scattering) of 47%, and at room temperature. The LS130 uses laser light at 750 nm to size particles from 0.1 μm to 900 μm diameter by light diffraction. The sample system pumps the suspension fluid with sample particles by vacuum through the diffraction sample cell where laser light is directed onto the particles for particle measurement. As the sample particles move through the diffraction sample cell, the collimated laser light is scattered, or diffracted, from each particle. A diffraction pattern is the pattern of scattered light intensity as a function of scattering angle, or simply the amount of light scattered by the different direction. Each particles diffraction pattern is characteristic of its size.

A 5-day, 1 L culture of P. fluorescens was used to inoculate 8 liters of YES medium supplemented with Impranil DLN. The culture was inoculated at room temperature under constant aeration. At the end of 5 days of incubation, little visible Impranil remained and the culture solids were removed by centrifugation (10,000×g, 20 min at 4°C). All remaining manipulations were also conducted at this temperature. The culture supernatant was concentrated 8-fold by ultrafiltration on a minitan high resolution tangential flow system fitted with a 10,000 mw cutoff membrane (Millipore). (NH4)2SO4 was added to the supernatant to give 60% saturation. After 30 min of stirring the precipitated proteins were collected by centrifugation (10,000× g, 15 min) and suspended in 50 mM phosphate buffer, pH 5.0 and dialyzed in 4 L of the same solution overnight.

The crude enzyme preparation was initially fractionated by anion exchange chromatography using a DEAE Sepharose CL–6B column (3×14 cm) with a bed volume of 53 ml. The column was equilibrated with 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 5.0). The enzyme activity was eluted in 17 min. No further activity was observed with a linear step-wise gradient of 0.1 to 1.0 M MgSO4. The polyurethanase activity was collected, pooled, and concentrated by ultrafiltration with a centripep-10 concentrator (Amicon).

The enzyme activity was further fractionated with a column (1.5×33 cm) of Sepharose G75–120 with a bed volume of 38 ml equilibrated with 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 5.0). A single peak of activity was detected. The final purification step involved a Sepharose 150–120 column (1.5×33 cm) with a bed volume of 38 ml equilibrated with 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 5.0). Polyurethanase activity was detected in Peak III and was determined to be 95% homogeneity as indicated by SDS–PAGE.
The Mr of the purified enzyme from Peak III was determined by a Dawn DSP–F Laser Photometer (Wyatt Technology) using a Zimm Plot method of determination.

After each step of the purification process, the purity of the enzyme was checked by polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE). Nondenaturing (ND) gels were run as described by Calza et al. (1985)with a 7% polyacrylamide resolving gel. Sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)– PAGE was performed as described by Laemmli (1970)with a 7% polyacrylamide resolving gel. Proteins were visualized by Coomassie blue staining.

During the purification, aliquots of the protein fractions were spotted on YES agarose plates (pH 5.0) supplemented with Impranil and observed for zones of clearing at 30°C. Assays for the characterization of the enzyme specificity with protease substrates using either 0.1% (wt/vol) azocall or 0.1% (wt/vol) hide powder azure (Chavira et al., 1984) or esterase activity with 8 mM p-nitrophenol-acetate, butyrate, or propionate (Deshpande et al., 1984) were performed as previously described (Howard et al., in press). All enzyme assays were determined to be linear with respect to time and protein concentration.
Impranil zymograms were performed as previously described (Howard et al., in press)
Protein concentration was determined by using a equation described by Kalb and Bernlohr (1977).

The enzyme preparation was treated with 10 mM EDTA for 1 hr prior to the assay. The EDTA was removed by filtration on a centricon 10 microconcentrator (Amicon). The preparation was washed three times with 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 5.0) before testing the effects of the divalent cations. All divalent cations were added as chloride salts and tested at a final concentration of 4 mM.
Inhibitors were incubated in the presence of the enzyme for 15 min(4°C) prior to the addition of the substrate (hide powder azure). Activity was determined as described above.

Impranilase activity by P. fluorescens. The ability of P. fluorescens to degrade the water dispersible polyurethane, Impranil, was tested either by inclusion of the substrate in YES agarose plates or defined YES agarose plates. After an appropriate incubation period at 30°C the agarose media was examined for zones of clearing around colonies (Fig. 1 ). Hydrolysis of the substrate could be visualized after approximately 16 h of incubation, with zones of clearing 1 cm in diameter around colonies. P. fluorescens grew quicker and more profusely in the richer YES medium as opposed to the defined YES medium (data not shown). Optimal conditions for Impranil hydrolysis by P. fluorescens was elucidated at different temperatures and pH. P. fluorescens was capable of hydrolyzing the Impranil substrate at 25°C, and 30°C with optimal hydrolysis at 25°C, zones of clearing approximately 3 cm, (data not shown). No growth occurred at 35°C or 40°C. In addition, P. fluorescens hydrolyzed the Impranil substrate at pH 5, 6, 7, and 8 with preeminent activity at pH 5. No activity was noted at pH 9 (data not shown).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Growth of P. fluorescens on Impranil
ce:section.ce:para: Since Impranil is a colloidal suspension and strict limitations are placed on the knowledge of its chemistry, conventional methods are impeded in determining the changes occurring during its degradation and growth of the bacterial cells utilizing it as a substrate. Thus, two instruments from Coulter Scientific, Inc. was employed to monitor substrate disappearance and cell growth. When P. fluorescens was grown on defined YES medium supplemented with Impranil, the amount of Impranil decreased with time. Fig. 2 shows the growth curve of P. fluorescens grown in defined YES medium supplemented with Impranil using the Multisizer II and the utilization of Impranil by the bacterial cells using the LS130. Increase in bacterial cell numbers were accomplished in the first 9 h of incubation, with a concentration of 3.05×109±0.14 cells·ml−1. The volume % of Impranil during this time course decreased from 47.18±0.48 to 10.4±0.12. Stationary phase of growth was noted for the remaining growing duration of 24 h and the volume % of Impranil further decreased to 0.023±0.003 during this time interval.

Polyurethane utilization by P. fluorescens followed simple Michaelis–Menten kinetics. Values for Ks and μ max for polyurethane utilization were elucidated by varying the Impranil concentration from 0.5 to 3.0 mg ml−1. From these results the values of Ks and μ max for polyurethane were estimated from the least-squares regression analysis of Lineweaver–Burke plots. The values for Ks and μ max were 0.9 mg ml−1 and 1.61 doublings h−1 respectfully with a regression coefficient of 0.961

The hydrolytic enzymes from P. fluorescens responsible for Impranil degradation were analyzed by Impranil zymograms using ND–PAGE gels. The Impranil zymogram revealed one slow migrating band, Rf 0.083. This band of activity was noted regardless of whether P. fluorescens was grown in LB medium or YES medium containing Impranil (data not shown). This suggests that only one major Impranilase polypeptide or an aggregate of proteins is produced and it is constitutively expressed.

P. fluorescens degrades 3 g·l−1 Impranil in 4 to 5 days. Once the Impranil containing medium was clear (little to no visible Impranil remaining), a crude enzyme preparation was made by concentrating the culture supernatant by ultrafiltration (10,000 Mr cutoff). The retentate contained all the detectable Impranilase activity. The ≥10,000 Mr retentate was (NH4)2SO4 saturated to 60% (wt/vol) and precipitated proteins were suspended in 50 mM phosphate buffer (pH 5.0) then dialyzed overnight.

The final purification step was Sephadex G150–120 gel filtration (Fig. 5 ). Peak III contained Impranilase activity (fractions 6–9). This protein fraction (Peak III) was used for further characterization. The purified enzyme could be stored at 4°C for at least one month without loss of activity or molecular weight.

The effect of divalent cations on the purified protein was examined by first treating the enzyme with a chelating agent (EDTA) to remove any endogenous divalent cations, followed by adding various divalent cations to the reaction mixture (Table 1 ). None of the divalent cations tested were stimulatory. Cu2, Mn2, and Zn2 were strongly inhibitory, while the remaining divalent cations tested showed either no effect or moderate levels of inhibition.

The influence of several commonly used inhibitors of protease activity was tested (Table 2 ). Phenylmethylsulfonylfluoride (PMSF) was inhibitory, whereas trypsin inhibitor (TI), bromelain inhibitor (BI), and N-tosyl-L-phenylalanine chloromethyl ketone (tPCK) were not inhibitory. Urethane had little if any effect on the enzyme, whereas the addition of Impranil inhibited the enzyme by 40%.

The purified protein was tested for the ability to hydrolyze various proteolytic substrates and aryl-esters at pH 5.0 (Table 3 ). Of the p-nitrophenyl ester substrates tested, none were hydrolyzed by the protein. Only the proteolytic substrates, azocall and hide powder azure were hydrolyzed, with activity against hide powder azure twice that of azocall.

Recycling of waste plastics has become very important because of shortages in raw materials for the synthesis of plastics. Due to the incompatibility of most polymers and the enormous difficulties encountered in segregating polymeric articles of different chemical composition found in plastic waste, complete recycling is difficult and limited to special cases. Hydrolytic processes are being contrived for the utilization of plastics scrap and waste as either an energy source or as raw material for the production of valuable chemicals (Schnabel, 1981). Huang and Roby (1986)observed that polyurethane degradation proceeded in a selective manner, with the amorphous regions being degraded prior to the crystalline regions. Also, it was observed that polyurethanes with long repeating units and hydrolytic groups would be less likely to pack into high crystalline regions as normal polyurethanes, and these polymers were more accessible to biodegradation. In the present study, P. fluorescens degraded Impranil with or without additional organic nutrients. In addition, exocellular proteins from P. fluorescens were also capable of hydrolyzing the polyurethane substrate in agarose plates. Also, P. fluorescens produced the polyurethane hydrolyzing activity without regard to the presence or absence of the substrate in the medium. When bacterial cells were grown on either LB medium or YES medium supplemented with Impranil, the polyurethanase activity was observed. P. fluorescens was capable of hydrolyzing the polyurethane substrate at pH 5, 6, 7, and 8 with preeminent activity at pH 5. P. chlororaphis also hydrolyzed the polyurethane substrate in the same pH range however, the preeminent activity was between pH 7 and 8 (Howard et al., in press). Very little if any attachment of bacterial cells to Impranil was observed unlike that of the Bacillus sp. (Blake et al., in press). However, the possibility of enzyme adhesion to the substrate has not been ruled out. The supernatant location of polyurethanase activity of cell growth indicates that the enzyme is secreted and constitutively expressed.

Values for Ks and μ max indicating growth parameters of P. fluorescens for polyurethane utilization were estimated to be 0.9 mg ml−1 and 1.6 h−1 respectfully. These values are similar to those observed for the utilization of polyurethane by Pseudomonas chlororaphis, Ks =0.8 mg ml−1 and μ max =1.32 h−1 (Howard et al., in press). These similarities indicate that the two microorganisms metabolize polyurethane very comparably however, the similarities between the cascade of polyurethanase proteins that the two bacteria process still remain to be elucidated. P. fluorescens and P. chlororaphis are genetically similar. Both microorganisms are in the Pseudomonas rRNA similarity group I, but are distinguished from each other by mol% G +C content of DNA P. fluorescens, 59.4–61.3, and P. chlororaphis, 63.5 (Palleroni, 1984). Also, unlike P. fluorescens, P. chlororaphis produces the pigment chlororaphin, utilizes benzoate but not arabinose or sorbitol.

Determination of the molecular weight of the purified protein as revealed by SDS–PAGE resulted in a single major protein band, with an apparent molecular weight of 29,000 daltons. Molecular weight determination of the purified protein using Rayleigh light scattering analysis indicated a molecular weight of 115,000 daltons, which is consistent with the ND–PAGE (apparent molecular weight of 116,000 Da). This data indicates that the protein could reside as a tetramer in the native form. The catalytic properties of the purified protein from P. fluorescens displayed only protease activity, and no esterase activity was observed using the substrates tested. The pH optimum of the enzyme was 5.0 and the enzyme activity was inhibited with the serine protease inhibitor PMSF.

The zone of clearing on Impranil agarose plates associated with the purified enzyme from P. fluorescens was of the beta-type. Similarly, in P. chlororaphis the beta zone of clearing was associated with a protease activity whereas the alpha zone of clearing was associated with an esterase activity (Howard et al., in press). Both of the enzyme activities were inhibited by PMSF. In addition, the molecular weight of the esterase from P. chlororaphis was determined to be 27 kDa with an optimum pH of 7.5. These results are similar to the alpha and beta-type zones of clearing observed by Crabbe et al. (1994). C. sengalensis was found to secrete an extracellular enzyme with esterase properties. This enzyme had a molecular weight of 28 kDa and was inhibited by PMSF. In addition, two types of polyurethane zones of clearing were produced by this fungal isolate, alpha and beta, a continuum of polyurethane-degradation from partial to complete. Interestingly, γ-chymotrypsin would also hydrolyze Impranil on an agarose plate (alpha-type zone of clearing) but neither chymotrypsin nor trypsin was capable of hydrolyzing the Impranil substrate (data not shown).

Wales and Sagar (1988)observed two peaks of esterase activities from Aspergillus terreus which were attributed to endopolyurethane and exopolyurethane esterase activity. The endopolyurethane activity resulted in a decrease in the degree of polymerization through the cleaving of bonds along the polymer chain. It was hypothesized that this enzyme affect could account for the alpha clearing where a weakly translucent zone was observed. Exopolyurethane activity which is involved in the removal of successive monomer units from the ends of the polymer chains could account for the visible clearing seen in the beta clearing zones. Interestingly, our data show that the protease activity from P. fluorescens and P. chlororaphis exhibits a beta-type of clearing whereas, the esterase activity exhibits an alpha-type of clearing.

The identification, purification, and characterization of enzymes are initial steps in elucidating the mechanism of polyurethane degradation. Studies are currently in progress of characterizing and purifying polyurethanase enzymes from Pseudomonas putida, Pseudomonas chlororaphis, Comamonas acidovorans, and two other Pseudomonads. Furthermore, molecular analysis are being implemented to determine the number of polyurethanase encoding genes each microorganism processes, and to gain a better understanding of the structure and function of these polyurethane-degrading enzymes.
